background: In August 2026, data centre operator CyrusOne was the target of a ShinyHunters "pay or leak" extortion attempt . The group subsequently published data allegedly obtained from the company, which included 373k unique email addresses across records relating to users, sales leads and CyrusOne employees. The data largely consisted of corporate contact information, including names, physical addresses, phone numbers and job titles.
It also included support tickets and other information related to the organisation's operations.
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
motive: In August 2026, data centre operator CyrusOne was the target of a ShinyHunters "pay or leak" extortion attempt .
outcome: Have I Been Pwned lists 373,460 email addresses in this breach record. An address total measures the source record's coverage.
The reported exposed data includes Email addresses, Employers, Job titles, Names, Phone numbers, Physical addresses, Support tickets.
editorial: A data centre operator's contact list is a map of who runs other companies' infrastructure. The people in this set are not random consumers: they are users of the platform, sales leads and CyrusOne employees, which means facilities managers, network engineers and the people who can authorise physical or remote access to servers. The field that makes this more than a contact list is support tickets.

Tickets at a data centre are where customers describe access requests, hardware changes and outages in their own words, sometimes naming the systems involved. Like any support record, they also capture whatever someone typed while trying to get a problem fixed quickly.

The realistic follow-on attack is social engineering aimed at the help desk, from either direction: someone posing as a customer to request access, or posing as CyrusOne staff to ask a customer to "confirm" credentials.

If you manage infrastructure hosted there, treat any unexpected access or credential request as suspect until it is verified through a channel you set up before this leak, and check whether your old tickets mention anything that should be rotated.

The extortion pattern in the record, a "pay or leak" demand followed by publication, is shared by a run of entries in this archive attributed to the same group, including McKesson , Crunchbase and Harvard . Read together, those records show the target was rarely consumer passwords. It was business relationship data: who works where, who buys what, and who to call. CyrusOne fits that shape exactly.

Physical addresses carry a particular weight for a data centre operator. Facility locations are often kept low-profile for security reasons, and a file that ties named engineers and customer contacts to sites and phone numbers gives anyone planning a pretext visit or a tailgating attempt a cast list.
Operators and tenants in this file should brief reception and security staff that a visitor who knows the right names is not, on that basis alone, expected or authorised.

fields.name: Physical addresses
fields.why: Where someone actually lives. Combined with a name this moves the risk off the internet.

fields.name: Phone numbers
fields.why: Enables SIM-swap attacks against SMS two-factor codes, and puts the number on scam-call lists indefinitely.

fields.name: Employers
fields.why: Connects a personal account to a workplace, which is how attackers pivot from a person to a company.

fields.name: Names
fields.why: Turns an anonymous address into an identified person, which is what makes targeted phishing possible.

fields.name: Email addresses
fields.why: An exposed address may be used in phishing attempts. Treat unexpected messages with caution.

fields.name: Job titles
fields.why: Identifies who has access to what, which is how targets for business email compromise are picked.

fields.name: Support tickets
fields.why: Adds detail to a profile that can be assembled from several breaches at once.

actions: Move two-factor authentication off SMS and onto an authenticator app, which a SIM swap cannot intercept.
Be sceptical of post and callers who already know your address, knowing it is no longer evidence of anything.
Be alert to phishing. A message may use details from exposed or collected records to appear familiar; verify requests through the service directly.
